--- title: "2.2 Marginal Effects with Nonlinearities" --- #### Marginal effect of *x~k~* for linear additive effects - The size of the effect *does not* depend on the value of *x~k~* - The size of the effect *does not* depend on the values of other IVs #### Marginal effect of *x~k~* for nonlinear interactive effects - The size of the effect *does* depend on the value of *x~k~* - The size of the effect *does* depend on the values of other IVs ### Nonlinear effects in linear regression models - By transforming IVs or the DV or by adding polynomial IVs the **effects** of IVs can be **nonlinear** even in the linear regression model - The *x*'s enter in the linear (additive) form **xβ** = β~0~ + β~1~*x*~1~ + β~2~*x*~2~ + ... - But the *x*'s can be **transformations** or **polynomials** of variables leading to nonlinear *effects*, e.g. *Square root*: $$\begin{aligned} y &= \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}\sqrt{w_{2}} + \varepsilon \\ &= \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2} + \varepsilon \end{aligned}$$ ***Polynomial***: $y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}{x_{1}}^{2} + \varepsilon$ **The effect in terms of the predictions is nonlinear** ### Polynomials of continuous IVs - Add a polynomial term for age - Note if you include a higher order polynomial (e.g., *age^2^*) in a regression model you need to also include the lower order terms (here, *age*) $${occupational\ prestige}_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{age}{age}_{i} + \beta_{{age}^{2}}{{age}^{2}}_{i} \ldots$$ ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(haven) # import Stata data and labels library(dplyr) # data manipulation library(ggplot2) # graphs library(modelsummary) # regression tables library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects library(cleanplots) # graph scheme cleanplots_defaults() gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta") # Keep only model vars and drop any missing data on them gss <- gss[c("occprest", "age", "woman", "college")] gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss), ] # Treat binary variables as factors using their value labels gss <- gss |> mutate(woman = as_factor(woman), college = as_factor(college)) age2mod <- lm(occprest ~ poly(age, 2, raw = TRUE) + woman + college, data = gss) modelsummary(age2mod, stars = c("*" = .05, "**" = .01, "***" = .001), title = "[2.2.a] Occupational prestige linear regression model") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

The *age^2^* coefficient is statistically significant---which is what we usually use to determine whether we should keep it in the model or not - If it was not significant, I would go back to a model with only *age* - The linear term (*age*) tells us the initial slope: here, a positive effect - The squared term (*age^2^*) tells us how the regression line's slope will change eventually: here, become more negative/less positive - The coefficients don't tell us at what age the effect becomes more negative; they do not tell us if the slope of age just becomes less positive or if it ever becomes negative (i.e., direction of effect reverses) - To answer these questions, we need to make and plot predictions ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} **Stata**: Use **margins** to calculate predictions, and [**marginsplot**](https://www.stata.com/features/overview/margins-plots/) to make the graph. **R**: Use [**plot_predictions**](https://marginaleffects.com/bonus/plot.html) function. ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . qui margins, at(age=(20(5)80)) . marginsplot, /// > recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(38(2)46) /// > title("[2.2.b] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age", siz > e(medium)) /// > subtitle("Quadratic Term for Age") /// > ytitle("Occupational Prestige") Variables that uniquely identify margins: age ``` ![](fig/cda-02_02_b-me_nonlinear-1.png){width=80% fig-alt="Predicted occupational prestige by age with a quadratic term: rising from age 20, peaking near 60, then falling slightly."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_predictions(age2mod, by = "age", newdata = datagrid(age = seq(20, 80, 5), grid_type = "counterfactual")) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(38, 46, 2), limits = c(38, 46)) + labs(title = "[2.2.b] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age", subtitle = "Quadratic Term for Age", x = "Age", y = "Occupational Prestige") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2-2-nonlinear-effects_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='Predicted occupational prestige by age with a quadratic term: rising from age 20, peaking near 60, then falling slightly.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: The marginal effect of age is now different depending on what starting and ending values are used to calculate ME~age~ ### Calculating marginal effects for nonlinear effects $$\widehat{occprest} = 31.36 + 0.28*{age}_{i} - 0.002*{{age}^{2}}_{i} - 0.165*{woman}_{i} + 16.25*{college}_{i}$$ - To calculate the marginal effect of age we must include a value of age in the linear term, and that same value squared for the quadratic term: Calculate the effect of aging from 40 to 50: $\widehat{occprest} = 31.36 + 0.28*40 - 0.002*1600 - 0.165*0 + 16.25*0$ = 39.36 $\widehat{occprest} = 31.36 + 0.28*50 - 0.002*2500 - 0.165*0 + 16.25*0$ = 40.36 40.36 -- 39.36 = 1.00 Calculate the effect of aging from 70 to 80: $\widehat{occprest} = 31.36 + 0.28*70 - 0.002*4900 - 0.165*0 + 16.25*0$ = 41.16 $\widehat{occprest} = 31.36 + 0.28*80 - 0.002*6400 - 0.165*0 + 16.25*0$ = 40.96 40.96 -- 41.16 = -0.20 ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . di 31.36 + 0.28*40 - 41.16 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] -0.2 ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Interpreting marginal effects for nonlinear effects Interpretation is now limited to the specific value of age the marginal effect is calculated at: > *For someone who is 40 years old, ten additional years of age is predicted to **increase** job prestige by about 1 point, accounting for other factors* > > *For someone who is 70 years old, ten additional years of age is predicted to **decrease** job prestige by about 0.2 points, accounting for other factors* ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} **Interpretation tip**: Note the initial clause specifying the starting age. These interpretations are only accurate for that specific age. ::: ## Summarizing nonlinear effects - A difficulty interpreting and presenting nonlinear effects is that the effect *depends* on where the effect is calculated \[i.e., starting and ending values\] and what type of change is being calculated - E.g., An instantaneous vs. one-unit vs. SD change will all yield different answers - And for categorical DVs, where the control variables are being held - How to summarize these effects? Two common solutions: - Marginal effect at the mean - Average marginal effect - **Marginal effect at the mean (MEM)**: what is the effect of a change in a focal IV *for the average person in your data* - **Average marginal effect (AME)**: on average---pooling and averaging across every observation in your data---what is the effect of a change in a focal IV ### Marginal effects at the mean/modes (MEM) - MEMs have often been used, perhaps due to ease of computation and tradition - For a MEM, hold all control variables in $\mathbf{x}_{- k}$ constant at their observed sample means/modes: $$MEM = \eta\left( x_{k} = end,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}} \right) - \eta\left( x_{k} = start,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}} \right)$$ - E.g., For a binary variable (e.g., *college*) make predictions at 0 and 1: $${MEM}_{binary} = \eta\left( x_{k} = 1,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}} \right) - \eta\left( x_{k} = 0,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}} \right)$$ - E.g., For a continuous variable (e.g., *age*) could compare predictions at any two places---e.g., one common approach is at the mean and at the mean + 1: $${MEM}_{continuous} = \eta\left( x_{k} = {\overline{x}}_{k} + 1,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}} \right) - \eta\left( x_{k} = {\overline{x}}_{k},\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}} \right)$$ ### Considerations for using a MEM - Is the mean/mode representative of what you want to know? - Is someone who is average on all variables realistic? Interesting? - If your theory suggests you should be looking at a specific type of person/observation (e.g., someone who is highly educated; someone who is working class; etc) then the effect for someone who is average on all characteristics may not accurately answer your question - Statistically, holding binary variables at their mean is not a problem - E.g., If ${\overline{x}}_{woman} = 0.60$, then the predictions are effectively weighted to reflect that 60% of the sample are women - However, substantively what does it mean to interpret a prediction for someone who is 0.60 a woman? - Stata will hold all variables, including binary/nominal variables, at their mean with the **atmeans** option. This is best practice and the way to get a true average effect - R's **marginaleffects** sets binary/nominal variables to their modes, which I do not like and does not produce an average effect ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . qui margins, at(age=(20(5)80)) . marginsplot, /// > title("[2.2.c] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age", siz > e(medium)) /// > subtitle("Quadratic Term for Age") /// > ytitle("Occupational Prestige") /// > recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) /// > ylab(38(2)46) xline(46) xline(63.50) /// > text(44 41 "mean of x") text(44 58 "mean + SD") Variables that uniquely identify margins: age ``` ![](fig/cda-02_02_c-me_nonlinear-2.png){width=80% fig-alt="The quadratic prediction line for age with vertical lines at the mean of age and one standard deviation above the mean."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_predictions(age2mod, by = "age", newdata = datagrid(age = seq(20, 80, 5), grid_type = "counterfactual")) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(46, 63.50)) + annotate("text", x = c(41, 58), y = 44, label = c("mean of x", "mean + SD")) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(38, 46, 2), limits = c(38, 46)) + labs(title = "[2.2.c] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age", subtitle = "Quadratic Term for Age", x = "Age", y = "Occupational Prestige") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2-2-nonlinear-effects_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='The quadratic prediction line for age with vertical lines at the mean of age and one standard deviation above the mean.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: Vertical lines on plot represent ${\overline{x}}_{age}$ and ${\overline{x}}_{age} + SD$ ### Calculating MEMs $$\widehat{occprest} = 31.36 + 0.28*{age}_{i} - 0.002*{{age}^{2}}_{i} - 0.165*{woman}_{i} + 16.25*{college}_{i}$$ - Calculate the marginal effect at the mean (MEM) for the effect of aging from the mean age (≈46) to a SD above the mean (age ≈63) while holding the control variables constant at their means: $$\widehat{occprest} = 31.36 + 0.28*46.17 - Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % 0.293 0.0576 5.08 <0.001 21.4 0.18 0.406 Term: age Type: response Comparison: 63.32191 - 46.165 ``` ::: ::: ::: > *For the average person in the data, a standard deviation increase in age (about 17.2 years) is associated with a 0.293 increase in occupational prestige points* > > OR > > *For someone who is average on all characteristics included in the model, an additional standard deviation of age (about 17.2 years) is predicted to increase occupational prestige by 0.293 points* ### Centered vs uncentered changes - The example above is an uncentered change: from *start* value to *start* + $\delta$ - $\delta$ = amount of change - Usually, and especially for larger changes like a SD, best to center the change on the *start* value $${ME}_{centered} = \eta\left( x_{k} = start + \frac{\delta}{2},\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x*} \right) - \eta\left( x_{k} = start - \frac{\delta}{2},\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x*} \right)$$ - Better represents the center of the distribution / values around the *start* value ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} **Stata**: [**mecompare**](/software/mecompare/index.qmd) centers all changes for continuous variables by default (**uncentered** is an option) **R**: [**avg_comparisons**](https://marginaleffects.com/man/r/comparisons.html) centers **sd** and **2sd** changes by default, but not \# changes (but, can request centered) ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . est restore opmod (results opmod are active now) . sum age if e(sample) Variable | Obs Mean Std. dev. SD/2", "mean + SD/2")) + labs(title = "[2.2.e] Distribution of age for workers in the GSS", subtitle = "Centered + SD change", x = "Age") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2-2-nonlinear-effects_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-alt='Histogram of age with vertical lines half a standard deviation below and above the mean.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Average marginal effects (AMEs) - We can compute a marginal effect for each observation in the data: $${ME}_{i} = \eta\left( x_{k} = {end}_{i},\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x}_{- k,i} \right) - \eta\left( x_{k} = {start}_{i},\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x}_{- k,i} \right)$$ - Note the subscript *i*'s in the formula which denote that the starting value, ending value, and control variable values can all vary across observations - $\mathbf{x}_{- k,i}$ indicates that the control variable values are set to the observed values for that observation - E.g., If you are making a prediction for the 1^st^ observation in the dataset who is a 45-year-old college educated woman, then make predictions at *age* = 45, *college* = 1, *woman* = 1 **for that observation** - Each ME calculation for each observation will use different values: those specific to that observation - For the *start* and *end* values: - The most common starting value is: whatever is observed - Common ending values for continuous IVs are: - Observed + 1 - Observed + SD - For binary IVs, ending value is: opposite of what was observed - A set of predictions at the *start* and *end* values is made for every single observation in the data - The difference between these two indicates the marginal effect for that specific observation (ME~i~) - The **average marginal effect** (AME) averages these effects over all observations in the data: $$AME = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i = 1}^{N}\left\{ \eta\left( x_{k} = {end}_{i},\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x}_{- k,i} \right) - \eta\left( x_{k} = {start}_{i},\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x}_{- k,i} \right) \right\}$$ - Interpretations of AMEs are less awkward than MEM because you can now simply say what the effect is "on average" as you have calculated the effect for every observation in your sample and then averaged ![](images/marginal-effect-meme.jpeg){width=40% fig-alt="Meme: 'You get a marginal effect! Everybody gets a marginal effect!'"} ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} [FYI if you don't get the reference](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pviYWzu0dzk) ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . est restore opmod (results opmod are active now) . mtable, at(age=(46.165 63.32191)) post Expression: Linear prediction, predict() | age xb ----------+------------------- 1 | 46.2 42.850 2 | 63.3 43.143 Specified values where .n indicates no values specified with at() | No at() ----------+--------- Current | .n . mlincom 2 - 1 | lincom pvalue ll ul -------------+--------------------------------------- 1 | 0.293 0.000 0.180 0.406 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(age2mod, variables = list(age = c(46.165, 63.32191))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. thus, it reflects both the effect (slope of line) and distribution of IV (where most of the data is) ### Estimating marginal effects ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata - In Stata, **margins**, **mchange**, and **mecompare** can all calculate marginal effects. [**mecompare**](/software/mecompare/index.qmd) has the most flexibility and capability - Default for all is AMEs; use option **atmeans** or **covariates(atmeans)** for MEMs ```{.stata-run} . est restore opmod (results opmod are active now) . mecompare age college, covariates(atmeans) Predicting: Linear prediction Marginal effects (N_m1=58304) | ME # Estimate SE P>|z| ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- age + 1 (centered) | m1 | 1 0.059 0.003 0.000 ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- college | College Deg - No Col Deg | m1 | 2 16.238 0.121 0.000 . mecompare age college note: models( ) omitted and e() holds a previous mecompare table; reusing the re > gress model from that run. Type mecompare with no arguments to replay the tabl > e instead. Predicting: Linear prediction Marginal effects (N_m1=58304) | ME # Estimate SE P>|z| ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- age + 1 (centered) | m1 | 1 0.059 0.003 0.000 ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- college | College Deg - No Col Deg | m1 | 2 16.238 0.121 0.000 ``` ## R - The [**marginaleffects**](https://marginaleffects.com/) package in R is extremely powerful, flexible, and works with [most any model](https://marginaleffects.com/bonus/supported_models.html) you can estimate in R\* - The **slopes** (MEM) and **avg_slopes** (AME) functions estimate instantaneous rates of change for continuous IVs - The **comparisons** (MEM) and **avg_comparisons** (AME) functions estimate effects for nominal/binary IVs, and can be used to estimate discrete changes for continuous IVs - For a MEM, specify that control variables be held at their mean/modes with: - **newdata = "mean"** - No special options needed for an AME as these are the default for the **avg\_** functions \*For more on MEs generally see [Mize and Han (2026)](/research/mize_han_hdma_2025.qmd); for more R examples see [marginaleffects.com](https://marginaleffects.com/) - Binary and nominal predictors work seamlessly with **avg_comparisons** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(age2mod, variables = "college") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % 16.2 0.121 134 <0.001 Inf 16 16.5 Term: college Type: response Comparison: College Degree - No Col Degree ``` ::: ::: - **avg_slopes** reports the average instantaneous rate of change ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_slopes(age2mod, variables = "age") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % 0.0589 0.00317 18.6 <0.001 253.8 0.0527 0.0651 Term: age Type: response Comparison: dY/dX ``` ::: ::: ::: > *On average, a one-year increase in age is predicted to increase occupational prestige by 0.059 points* > > *Workers with college degrees have jobs that are about 16 points more prestigious than workers without college degrees* ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata #### Custom changes with the mecompare command - **mecompare** defaults to a one-unit change for continuous IVs - Can specify various custom amounts, e.g., a standard deviation with **amount(sd)**, or a specific $\delta$ with **amount(#)**, or an instantaneous rate of change with **amount(rate)** ```{.stata-run} . mecompare age, amount(sd) note: models( ) omitted and e() holds a previous mecompare table; reusing the re > gress model from that run. Type mecompare with no arguments to replay the tabl > e instead. Predicting: Linear prediction Marginal effects (N_m1=58304) | ME # Estimate SE P>|z| ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- age + SD (centered) | m1 | 1 1.010 0.054 0.000 ``` ## R #### Customizing amounts of change with marginaleffects - [**avg_comparisons**](https://marginaleffects.com/man/r/comparisons.html) has some built-in amounts you can specify for an average marginal effect with continuous IVs - E.g., Specify **sd** for one standard deviation or **2sd** for two standard deviations, or specify any custom $\delta$ amount by listing the number ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(age2mod, variables = list(age = "sd")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % 1.01 0.0543 18.6 <0.001 253.8 0.904 1.12 Term: age Type: response Comparison: (x + sd/2) - (x - sd/2) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(age2mod, variables = list(age = 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % 0.233 0.0148 15.8 <0.001 184.4 0.205 0.262 Term: age Type: response Comparison: +5 ``` ::: ::: - A quirk is that **sd** and **2sd** are centered by default, but a custom $\delta$ amount is not - Set centered changes as the default for all changes with ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} options(marginaleffects_contrast_direction = "center") avg_comparisons(age2mod, variables = list(age = 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % 0.294 0.0158 18.6 <0.001 253.8 0.263 0.325 Term: age Type: response Comparison: +5 ``` ::: ::: ::: > *On average, a standard deviation increase in age (about 17.2 years) is predicted to increase occupational prestige by about 1 point* ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} **Interpretation tip**: The first time you report a +SD marginal effect, good practice to remind readers of the size of a SD. This will vary drastically across samples and is needed to contextualize the effect. :::
